agent_notes: The superscription 'of David' is verse 1 here (KJV 37:0, 37:1 share the Hebrew verse). The psalm is an alphabetic acrostic, loosely: אל (1), בטח (3), גול (5), דום (7), הרף (8), ועוד (10), זומם (12). I mention it once, here, as my own observation; no commentary in the packet says so.

תִּתְחַר: Rashi, Radak and Meiri read it as a verb of 'contending/mixing in' (cf. Jer 12:5, 'how will you compete with horses'); Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Malbim also allow the root חרה 'to burn, be angry'. STEPBible's 'fret' follows the second. I kept 'fret' in the literal layer, which keeps the burning image, and gave both options in the note.

ארץ is 'land' throughout vv. 3, 9, 11 (the KJV varies between 'land' in v3 and 'earth' in vv. 9 and 11). I used 'land' everywhere in the literal layer. The echo in Matthew 5:5 reads the verse with 'earth'; I note it in the commentary but do not import it.

Meiri on 'gnashing' as scoffing/mockery and Ibn Ezra on 'gnashing in anticipation of the grab' are interpretive extensions; I cite them as what they are, and rely on the plain sense (teeth grinding in malice) for the dramatic layer.

agent_notes: The Hebrew has 'adonay (Lord), not YHWH, here; I kept 'my Lord' in the literal layer and 'the Lord' in the dramatic one. 'His' day has no stated antecedent; the previous verse (the wicked plotting against the righteous) is not in the packet, so I left 'him' as the plotter without naming him.

agent_notes: Rashi's reading (Abraham's few men against Amraphel's host) is a midrashic application and I cite it only as such. Radak and Ibn Ezra take hamon as 'wealth' (cf. Eccl 5:9); I follow them over 'multitude'. The adjective rabbim ('many') is grammatically plural against singular hamon, which Radak discusses.
Reviewer request applied: translation_literal no longer adds 'the Lord'; the divine name appears once, as YHWH, at the end, keeping the Hebrew order (sustaining the righteous, then YHWH).

The five English versions all put the divine subject first ('the LORD upholdeth'); the Hebrew holds the name for the last word. The dramatic layer keeps that delay. Ibn Ezra's reading of זרועות as the arms that draw the bow is taken from the packet; the dramatic layer does not assert it, since the verse does not say bows.

(or '... and the righteous are sustained by YHWH'), with the name once. (PS.37.17: וְסוֹמֵךְ צַדִּיקִים יְהוָה, 'and sustaining righteous ones YHWH' (YLT: 'And Jehovah is sustaining the righteous'))

agent_notes: Disputed: yiqar karim. Rashi offers morning mist over a plain or fattened lambs; Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read the fat of lambs burnt on the altar; Ibn Ezra also records 'pasture grass'. I chose 'the splendour of the pastures/lambs' in the literal layer, keeping the ambiguity of karim, and 'fat of lambs' (as KJV, ASV) in the dramatic layer, flagged in the commentary. The two kalu are glossed identically to keep the repetition visible.

Ambiguity of the subject of 'he delights': most take YHWH delighting in the man's way (Radak, Metzudat David); Ibn Ezra's note is obscure and I do not rely on it. YLT takes the man as subject. I follow YHWH.

yutal is a Hophal of tul, 'be hurled'. KJV 'utterly' has no word in the Hebrew; it harmonizes to Radak's 'not thrown to the ground completely'. Ibn Ezra's 'and some say: falls in his thought' not used.

STEPBible glosses נֶעֱזָב as 'forsaken'; kept, but 'abandoned' would match the root עזב used in vv. 28 and 33 and the literal layer uses 'forsaken' throughout so the repetition stays visible. The KJV 'begging' for מְבַקֶּשׁ is an interpretation; the verb is simply 'seeking' (the same root as 'seeks to kill him' in v. 32), and Radak and Meiri disagree on how much lack the verse allows.

agent_notes: וּרְעֵה אֱמוּנָה is genuinely split: 'feed on faithfulness' (ASV, Rashi), 'cultivate/tend faithfulness' (shepherd as keeper, Ibn Ezra), 'befriend faithfulness', and KJV's 'verily thou shalt be fed' (taking אֱמוּנָה adverbially). I render 'and graze [on] faithfulness' literally and give the options in the commentary.

Per the reviewer request, the earlier sentence about the KJV leaving out 'he' is gone. The commentary now says only that the KJV renders the Niphal correctly. The claim in the note on yarshi'enu rests on Radak and Metzudat David reading the verse as a trial before the ruler; the courtroom setting at the gate is my own reading of the ancient context.

Radak and Metzudat David take 'in his hand' as the wicked man's hand, which I follow. The BBE has 'their hands', a plural the Hebrew does not have. I kept 'abandon' for 'azav in the literal layer, where STEPBible also has it.

agent_notes: קַוֵּה is glossed 'wait with hope'. The root is also the rope (קַו) image; I mention it only lightly because the connection is common but not certain for this verse.

agent_notes: אֶזְרָח is the hard word. The KJV 'green bay tree' comes from the older versions' 'cedar' tradition and is not in the Hebrew. I glossed it 'native' (as in Lev 24:16) and put '[tree]' in brackets in the literal layer, following Metzudat Zion; Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it as a person with a large family, and Rashi as one rooted in the land with possessions. The five English versions split three ways and I chose the plainest Hebrew sense. מִתְעָרֶה is also uncertain: 'spreading himself' (KJV, YLT) versus 'rooted' (Rashi, Metzudat Zion); I gloss it 'baring/spreading himself' and mention both.

The Masoretic text reads וַיַּעֲבֹר 'and he passed', in the third person, while the next clause switches to 'I sought him'. I believe the Septuagint and some other ancient versions read the first verb as first person ('and I passed by'), which would make the speaker the one who goes past and finds the tree gone; I have not checked this against the manuscripts, so it is stated only in my own words with no source. The translation follows the Hebrew as pointed.

(PS.37.15: five words; PS.37.36 ASV in the packet: 'But one passed by')

agent_notes: KJV 'perfect man' and ASV 'man of peace' split on tam and on the last clause. I read אחרית as 'a future, an afterward' that belongs to the person (לְאִישׁ), and שלום as the content of that future, not as a description of a 'man of peace'. Ibn Ezra's reading of 'tam' and 'yashar' as persons is followed; Malbim's afterlife reading is later and I did not build it into the text.

history.note: [consider] Pick one parsing for both layers (or keep 'man of peace' in the literal and say in the commentary that the dramatic layer follows the KJV/Targum reading). (PS.37.37: כִּי־אַחֲרִית לְאִישׁ שָׁלוֹם; KJV 'the end of that man is peace', ASV 'a happy end to the man of peace')

agent_notes: The perfect נִשְׁמְדוּ and נִכְרְתָה are rendered as prophetic perfects ('are destroyed', 'is cut off'); YLT puts them in the past, KJV in the future. The Hebrew form allows both, and the sentence is a general truth. I kept the English present-perfect in the literal layer and flagged it.
The STEPBible gloss for עַל is 'on'; KJV and ASV have 'in'. I kept 'upon' in the literal layer because Rashi and Metzudat David read על as 'upon the support (מִשְׁעֶנֶת) of the LORD'.

The Hebrew has both וַיְפַלְּטֵם (wayyiqtol) and יְפַלְּטֵם (yiqtol) side by side. The doubling is in the text as pointed; Radak reads it as emphasis on the abundance of help. I translate both and keep them visible. STEPBible glosses the second as 'he delivers them'; I made the sequence 'delivered ... delivers' to show the shift of tense.
STEPBible glosses חָסוּ 'they have taken refuge'; I gloss it 'they took refuge' to match the narrative past of the verse. The root חסה is the shelter image, which KJV 'trust' flattens.

וְהִתְחוֹלֵל: the commentators split between 'wait longingly' (from יחל/תוחלת: Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat) and 'writhe, as a woman in labour' (from חיל: Ibn Ezra's preferred reading, also Radak's alternative). The literal layer takes 'wait longingly'; the 'writhe' reading appears only in the gloss and the commentary.
STEPBible glosses דּוֹם 'be still' and the five English versions say 'rest'/'be silent'. Root דמם is silence first (cf. Lev 10:3 as Rashi cites it), so I translate 'be silent' and keep 'rest' out.

notes.note: Commentators on this window are cited by name and verse as they appear in the packet; Psalm 37 is an alphabetic acrostic and several verses here open with successive letters (v. 25 nun, v. 27 samekh, v. 30 pe, v. 32 tsade, v. 34 qof, v. 35 resh). I mention the acrostic only where it explains the compressed, proverb-like style.
